title: Sagas & Distributed Transactions
subtitle: Watch one order touch three services, see why a global lock breaks, and see how a saga undoes work instead.
learn: Why two-phase commit (2PC) blocks and why most microservice teams avoid it
How a saga replaces one big transaction with a chain of small local ones
The difference between orchestration and choreography, and when each fits
How compensating actions undo earlier steps, and why they must be idempotent
What a saga cannot give you: isolation between concurrent sagas

steps.title: One order, three databases
steps.body: A customer places an order. That means charging a card (Payment DB), reserving stock (Inventory DB), and booking a courier (Shipping DB). Each service owns its own database, so no single BEGIN ... COMMIT covers all three. What happens if the card is charged but the courier booking fails? This lesson is about keeping those three writes consistent without one shared transaction.
steps.idea: Once data is split across services, a single ACID transaction no longer spans the whole business operation.
steps.caption: Three services, three private databases.

steps.title: The classic answer: two-phase commit
steps.body: Two-phase commit adds a coordinator. In phase one it asks every participant to PREPARE: do the work, take locks, and promise you can commit. In phase two, if all said yes, it tells everyone to COMMIT; otherwise ABORT. With 5 ms round trips this takes roughly 10 to 20 ms, and the rows stay locked the whole time. Here the Order service plays coordinator.
steps.idea: 2PC gives all-or-nothing atomicity by making every participant hold locks until the coordinator decides.
steps.caption: Coordinator collects three PREPARE votes.

steps.title: Why 2PC hurts at scale
steps.body: Suppose the coordinator crashes after collecting the YES votes but before sending its decision. Every participant is now stuck: it promised to commit, so it cannot unilaterally abort, and it must keep its locks until the coordinator returns. Orders on those rows queue up behind the locks. Add the fact that all services must be up at once and speak a compatible protocol (such as XA), and availability becomes the product of every participant's uptime.
steps.idea: 2PC is a blocking protocol: a coordinator failure freezes locks across every service, and availability multiplies down.
steps.caption: Coordinator died; three services hold locks.

steps.title: The saga idea
steps.body: A saga drops the global lock. It splits the business operation into a sequence of local transactions, one per service. Each commits immediately and releases its locks. If a later step fails, the saga runs a compensating action for every step already done, such as refunding a payment. The data is briefly inconsistent while the saga runs, and that is the price: you trade atomicity and isolation for availability.
steps.idea: A saga is a series of local commits plus a planned undo for each, giving eventual consistency instead of atomicity.
steps.caption: Each step commits alone and frees its locks.

steps.title: Orchestration: a conductor drives it
steps.body: In an orchestrated saga one component, here the Order service, holds the workflow. It sends a command to Payment, waits for the reply, then commands Inventory, then Shipping. The order of steps and the failure rules live in one place, often a persisted state machine, so it can resume after a crash. Each service just does its local job and answers.
steps.idea: Orchestration puts the saga's flow in one place that tells each service what to do next.
steps.caption: Orchestrator commands each step in turn.

steps.title: A step fails: run the undo steps
steps.body: Shipping finds no courier is available and replies with a failure. Its own transaction rolled back, so there is nothing to undo there. The orchestrator now walks backwards: release the reserved stock, then refund the charge. A compensation is a new forward action, not a database rollback, because the earlier steps already committed. A refund appears on the customer's statement, so design compensations as part of the business, not as an afterthought.
steps.idea: Compensating actions are new transactions that semantically reverse committed steps, run in reverse order.
steps.caption: Failure triggers refund and stock release.

steps.title: Choreography: services react to events
steps.body: The alternative has no conductor. Payment publishes PaymentTaken on the event bus. Inventory reacts and publishes StockReserved, Shipping reacts to that, and so on. Every service knows only which events it listens to and emits. There is no central point of failure, and adding a listener needs no change to the others, but nobody holds the whole flow.
steps.idea: Choreography encodes the saga as a chain of events, with no central coordinator and no single place that shows the whole flow.
steps.caption: Events pass the baton through the bus.

steps.title: Choosing between the two
steps.body: As a rule of thumb, choreography suits short sagas of two to four steps with few owners, because it is simple and loosely coupled. Past that, the event chain becomes hard to follow and cyclic dependencies creep in, so orchestration pays off: one place to read, test, time out, and monitor the flow. Orchestrators add a component to run and can attract business logic, so keep them to sequencing only. Failures travel the bus too, as events.
steps.idea: Choreography wins on coupling for small flows; orchestration wins on visibility once flows grow or branch.
steps.caption: A failure event triggers the undo.

steps.title: Retries, duplicates, and dirty reads
steps.body: Messages are usually delivered at least once, so every step and every compensation must be idempotent: refunding twice must not refund twice, so key each command with the saga and step ID. And since each step is visible the moment it commits, another request can see an item as reserved before the order finally succeeds. Teams handle this with semantic locks, such as a PENDING status flag.
steps.idea: Sagas need idempotent steps and explicit handling of intermediate state, because they offer no isolation.
steps.caption: Duplicate refund command is ignored.

steps.title: Atomic, or available
steps.body: 2PC gives atomic commits across services but blocks on coordinator failure and holds locks, so it is rare between microservices. A saga gives up atomicity and isolation: each local transaction commits, and failures trigger compensations in reverse order. Pick orchestration for longer or branching flows and choreography for short ones. Make every step idempotent and plan for intermediate states.
steps.idea: Replace one big lock with small commits and planned undo steps, and design for the in-between.
steps.caption: Local commits plus compensations.

quiz.q: A 2PC coordinator crashes after all participants voted YES but before it sent COMMIT. What is the main problem?
options: Participants abort immediately and the order is lost
Participants must keep their locks and wait, since they cannot decide alone
Participants commit on their own after a short timeout
The votes are replayed from the event bus
quiz.why: Having voted YES, a participant promised it can commit and cannot safely abort or commit without the decision, so it blocks while holding locks.

quiz.q: In a saga, the payment step has committed and the shipping step then fails. What is the correct recovery?
options: Roll back the payment database transaction
Retry shipping forever and leave payment as is
Run a compensating action such as a refund
Delete the payment row directly from the Payment DB
quiz.why: The payment transaction already committed and released its locks, so it cannot be rolled back. A new forward action, the refund, reverses its business effect.

quiz.q: Your saga has seven steps with conditional branches and the team keeps losing track of where an order is stuck. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to choreography so each service owns less
Use 2PC for the last three steps
Remove all compensations to simplify it
Move to orchestration with a persisted workflow state
quiz.why: Orchestration puts the flow and its current state in one place, which makes long or branching sagas readable, testable, and monitorable.

quiz.q: A refund command is delivered twice because of a retry. Why is that safe in a well-built saga?
options: The event bus guarantees exactly-once delivery everywhere
The refund is idempotent, keyed by saga and step ID
Sagas hold a global lock during compensation
The customer is refunded twice, then reconciled monthly
quiz.why: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen, so each step and compensation must detect a repeat via an idempotency key and do nothing the second time.

cheatsheet.def: Coordinator asks all participants to PREPARE, then COMMIT or ABORT. Atomic, but blocking and lock-heavy.
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action, giving eventual consistency across services.
A central orchestrator sends commands to each step and owns the flow and failure rules. Better for long flows.
Services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. Loosely coupled, but the flow is implicit.
A new transaction that semantically undoes a committed step, such as a refund. Run in reverse order.
An ID sent with each command so a duplicate delivery is recognised and ignored.
A status flag like PENDING that marks data as mid-saga so other requests treat it carefully.
The step after which the saga must complete forward, because later steps cannot be compensated.
